claim: In Homo sapiens, body odour contains 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (3M3SH) as a key chemical component.
source: In Homo sapiens, this is now recognised as body odour, a key chemical component of which is the sulphurous thioalcohol, 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (3M3SH).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the chemical composition of human body odour.

claim: Volatile 3M3SH is produced in the underarm as a result of specific microbial activity.
source: Volatile 3M3SH is produced in the underarm as a result of specific microbial activity, which act on the odourless dipeptide-containing malodour precursor molecule, S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH, secreted in the axilla (underarm) during colonisation.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract as a description of how 3M3SH is produced.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is an odourless dipeptide-containing malodour precursor molecule secreted in the axilla.
source: Volatile 3M3SH is produced in the underarm as a result of specific microbial activity, which act on the odourless dipeptide-containing malodour precursor molecule, S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH, secreted in the axilla (underarm) during colonisation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract describing the precursor molecule.

claim: Staphylococcus hominis transports S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
source: Here we report the structural and biochemical basis of bacterial transport of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH by Staphylococcus hominis, which is converted to the sulphurous thioalcohol component 3M3SH in the bacterial cytoplasm, before being released into the environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is converted to 3M3SH in the bacterial cytoplasm of Staphylococcus hominis.
source: Here we report the structural and biochemical basis of bacterial transport of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH by Staphylococcus hominis, which is converted to the sulphurous thioalcohol component 3M3SH in the bacterial cytoplasm, before being released into the environment.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as part of the metabolic pathway.

claim: 3M3SH is released into the environment after conversion in bacterial cytoplasm.
source: Here we report the structural and biochemical basis of bacterial transport of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH by Staphylococcus hominis, which is converted to the sulphurous thioalcohol component 3M3SH in the bacterial cytoplasm, before being released into the environment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the final step in the process.

claim: The axilla provides a unique niche for bacteria in Homo sapiens.
source: In Homo sapiens the skin of the underarm (axilla) provides a unique niche for bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: The axilla environment is nutrient-rich through secretions of various glands.
source: Through the secretions of various glands, that open onto the skin or into hair follicles, this environment is nutrient-rich and hosts a unique microbial community (Taylor et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Esterified fatty acids and other lipids are secreted by the sebaceous gland.
source: Esterified fatty acids and other lipids are secreted by the sebaceous gland, while the eccrine glands produce a dilute salt solution with lactate and other organic solutes being secreted (Bovell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Eccrine glands produce a dilute salt solution with lactate and other organic solutes.
source: Esterified fatty acids and other lipids are secreted by the sebaceous gland, while the eccrine glands produce a dilute salt solution with lactate and other organic solutes being secreted (Bovell, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The apocrine gland is found only in the axilla, areolae, genitalia and external auditory meatus.
source: A third exocrine gland, the apocrine, which is more specialized and found only in the axilla, areolae, genitalia and external auditory meatus (ear canal) (Collins, 1989), starts secreting an odourless lipid-rich viscous secretion with the onset of puberty (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The apocrine gland starts secreting an odourless lipid-rich viscous secretion with the onset of puberty.
source: A third exocrine gland, the apocrine, which is more specialized and found only in the axilla, areolae, genitalia and external auditory meatus (ear canal) (Collins, 1989), starts secreting an odourless lipid-rich viscous secretion with the onset of puberty (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing apocrine gland function.

claim: The lipid rich secretion from apocrine glands is not involved in thermoregulation.
source: The lipid rich secretion is not involved in thermoregulation like the eccrine gland and in mammals has a likely role in scent generation (Collins, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Apocrine secretion in mammals has a likely role in scent generation.
source: The lipid rich secretion is not involved in thermoregulation like the eccrine gland and in mammals has a likely role in scent generation (Collins, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The link between the axillary apocrine gland, underarm bacteria and body odour was first recognised over 50 years ago.
source: In humans, the link between the axillary apocrine gland, underarm bacteria and body odour (BO), was first recognised over 50 years ago (Shelley et al., 1953)
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Early culture-based studies found the axillary microbiota to be dominated by Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and Propionibacterium species.
source: early culture-based studies on this relationship found the axillary microbiota to be dominated by Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and Propionibacterium species, with the Corynebacteria in particular correlating with malodour intensity (Taylor et al., 2003; Leyden et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Corynebacteria correlate with malodour intensity.
source: early culture-based studies on this relationship found the axillary microbiota to be dominated by Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and Propionibacterium species, with the Corynebacteria in particular correlating with malodour intensity (Taylor et al., 2003; Leyden et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Culture-independent meta-taxonomic studies confirmed that the axilla is dominated by Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium and Propionibacterium genera.
source: More recent culture-independent meta-taxonomic studies have confirmed that the axilla is dominated by these genera, although the presence of additional taxa not previously indicated by culture-based methods is also evident, notably Gram-positive anaerobic cocci (GPAC) belonging to the Anaerococcus and Peptoniphilus genera (Costello et al., 2009; Egert et al., 2011; Troccaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Gram-positive anaerobic cocci belonging to Anaerococcus and Peptoniphilus genera are present in the axilla.
source: More recent culture-independent meta-taxonomic studies have confirmed that the axilla is dominated by these genera, although the presence of additional taxa not previously indicated by culture-based methods is also evident, notably Gram-positive anaerobic cocci (GPAC) belonging to the Anaerococcus and Peptoniphilus genera (Costello et al., 2009; Egert et al., 2011; Troccaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: 16-androstenes are now believed to be only minor contributors to axillary malodour.
source: However, 16-androstenes are now believed to be only minor contributors to axillary malodour (James et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The VFAs most heavily involved in body odour are a series of structurally-unusual medium-chain (C6-C10) acids originating from N-acylglutamine precursors present in apocrine sweat.
source: it is accepted that the VFAs most heavily involved in BO are a series of structurally-unusual medium-chain (C6-C10) acids originating from N-acylglutamine precursors present in apocrine sweat (Natsch et al., 2003; Natsch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Thioalcohols have been identified as important components of human body odour.
source: A third class of molecule, the thioalcohols (also called sulfanylalkanols), have recently been identified as important components of human body odour and a number of these have been detected within the volatiles released from the underarm (Troccaz et al., 2004; Natsch et al., 2004; Hasegawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Thioalcohols are particularly pungent and can be detected in pg.l−1 quantities.
source: They are particularly pungent and can be detected in pg.l−1 quantities, an order of magnitude lower than many other volatile chemicals emanating from the skin (Natsch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: 3M3SH is the most abundant and pungent thioalcohol.
source: The most abundant and pungent of these thioalcohols is 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (3M3SH) (Figure 1B), which is a primary causal molecule of axillary malodour and subsequent BO (Troccaz et al., 2004; Hasegawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: 3M3SH is a primary causal molecule of axillary malodour and subsequent body odour.
source: The most abundant and pungent of these thioalcohols is 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (3M3SH) (Figure 1B), which is a primary causal molecule of axillary malodour and subsequent BO (Troccaz et al., 2004; Hasegawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Thioalcohols are released as a peptide-conjugated precursor from the apocrine gland.
source: Thioalcohols are known to be released as a peptide-conjugated precursor from the apocrine gland, which secretes directly into the hair follicle (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Thioalcohol precursors are thought to be secreted into the axilla via the ABC transporter ABCC11 as odourless glutathione conjugates.
source: The biosynthetic origin of the thioalcohol precursors is currently poorly understood, but they are thought to be secreted into the axilla via the ABC transporter ABCC11 as odourless glutathione conjugates (Baumann et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: The glutathione conjugated form (SG-3M3SH) has never been detected in axillary sweat.
source: The glutathione conjugated form (SG-3M3SH) has never been detected in axillary sweat; however, the L-cysteinylglycine dipeptide conjugated form, S-[1-(2-hydroxyethyl)−1-methylbutyl]-L-cysteinylglycine (S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH) (Figure 1B), is readily detectable (Starkenmann et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is readily detectable in axillary sweat.
source: The glutathione conjugated form (SG-3M3SH) has never been detected in axillary sweat; however, the L-cysteinylglycine dipeptide conjugated form, S-[1-(2-hydroxyethyl)−1-methylbutyl]-L-cysteinylglycine (S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH) (Figure 1B), is readily detectable (Starkenmann et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT1) localises to the apocrine sweat gland and converts SG-3M3SH to S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
source: recently a γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT1) has been demonstrated to localise to the apocrine sweat gland and convert SG-3M3SH to S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH (Baumann et al., 2014a) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH can be taken up and metabolised by Staphylococcus hominis, Staphylococcus haemolyticus and Staphylocooccus lugdunensis to liberate 3M3SH.
source: We and others have demonstrated that S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH can be taken up and metabolised by a highly limited range of staphylococcal species present in the axilla, namely Staphylococcus hominis, Staphylococcus haemolyticus and Staphylocooccus lugdunensis, to liberate 3M3SH, that subsequently exits the cell through an undefined mechanism (Troccaz et al., 2004; Starkenmann et al., 2005; Bawdon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: A strong correlation between S. hominis and body odour production has been established using culture-independent taxonomic studies.
source: A strong correlation between S. hominis and body odour production has recently been established using culture-independent taxonomic studies of the axillary microbiota (Troccaz et al., 2015), confirming the biological significance of this low-abundance species within the axilla in BO production in humans.
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the introduction.

claim: Resting cells of E. coli are able to remove S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine from solution and break it down to release benzyl mercaptan.
source: Resting cells of E. coli were indeed able to remove S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine from solution and break it down to release the thiol active product, benzyl mercaptan (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figures showing experimental data.

claim: TnaA is capable of releasing benzyl mercaptan from S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine.
source: Interestingly, TnaA which is a tryptophanase known to have L-cysteine desulfhydrase activity (Awano et al., 2005) is also capable of releasing benzyl mercaptan.
evidence: This is stated with citation support in the results section.

claim: Disruption of tnaA led to an almost complete loss of biotransformation of S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine.
source: Individual disruption of metC and malY did not decrease the amount of benzyl mercaptan produced by E. coli, while disruption of tnaA led to an almost complete loss of biotransformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figure showing experimental data.

claim: E. coli takes up S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine, whereupon a host dipeptidase cleaves the glycine residue prior to cleavage of the S-benzyl-cysteine by TnaA to release benzyl mercaptan.
source: This suggests that E. coli takes up the S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine, whereupon a host dipeptidase cleaves the glycine residue prior to cleavage of the S-benzyl-cysteine by TnaA to release the benzyl mercaptan.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Benzyl mercaptan production in E. coli ΔDB1 strain (ΔoppC ΔdppC) was similar to the wild-type strain.
source: Surprisingly, benzyl mercaptan production was similar to the wild-type strain, suggesting that neither ABC transporter was important for Cys-Gly-conjugate transport (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The dtpB deletion strain had an overall 50% drop in thiol production from S-benzyl-L-cysteinylglycine.
source: Most of these strains had similar levels of benzyl mercaptan production to the wild-type, with the exception of dtpB which had an overall 50% drop in thiol production (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: Transporters belonging to the POT family are most likely responsible for Cys-Gly-conjugate transport in E. coli.
source: These data suggest that transporters belonging to the POT family are most likely responsible for Cys-Gly-conjugate transport, revealing a new biological role for bacterial POT transporters in the uptake of Cys-Gly-(S) conjugates.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The dtpB gene alone was able to confer a malodour production (BO+) phenotype to E. coli.
source: Consistent with the reduction in benzyl mercaptan production reported in Figure 2A, the dtpB gene alone was able to confer a malodour production (BO+) phenotype to E. coli, which was not seen with any of the other dtp genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: S. hominis contains only a single POT family member DtpT (SH1446).
source: Unlike E. coli, S. hominis contains only a single POT family member DtpT (SH1446), orthologues of which were seen in all sequenced staphylococci (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figure.

claim: SH0415 is only present in S. hominis and S. haemolyticus.
source: We also identified a second system, encoded by STAHO0001_0415 (SH0415), which is annotated as an MFS transporter and only present in S. hominis and S. haemolyticus, two known thioalcohol producers, and which is genetically linked to genes involved in peptide and amino acid metabolism (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Uptake of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH was only enhanced by the presence of SH1446, with SH0415 having little effect.
source: When levels of 3M3SH production were measured in these strains, uptake was only enhanced by the presence of SH1446, with SH0415 having little effect on 3M3SH activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH transporter in S. hominis is the POT transporter STAH0001_1446 (SH1446).
source: Together these data strongly support the conclusion that the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH transporter in S. hominis is the POT transporter STAH0001_1446 (SH1446).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Di- and tri-Ala peptides inhibit 3M3SH production in E. coli expressing SH1446.
source: Firstly, we used our E. coli system where 3M3SH production is seen when SH1446 is expressed in trans and we observed clear inhibition of 3M3SH production with both di- and tri-Ala peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figure showing experimental data.

claim: The purified TnaA enzyme that cleaves Cys-3M3SH was not inhibited by di- and tri-Ala peptides.
source: The purified TnaA enzyme that cleaves Cys-3M3SH was not inhibited by any of these peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supporting figure showing experimental data.

claim: PepTSh is a proton coupled peptide transporter.
source: Acidification of the lumen of the liposome was observed in the presence of a membrane potential (ΔΨ, negative inside), and addition of external di- or tri-peptide substrate, demonstrating that PepTSh is a proton coupled peptide transporter.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claim: Acidification was observed in the presence of the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH precursor peptide, confirming PepTSh as the transporter for this molecule in S. hominis.
source: Importantly we also observed acidification in the presence of the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH precursor peptide, confirming our earlier identification of PepTSh as the transporter for this molecule in S. hominis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claim: The IC50 value for tri-alanine binding to PepTSh is 23.7 ± 3.4 μM.
source: The IC50 value for tri-alanine, di-alanine and Cys-Gly were 23.7 ± 3.4, 72.2 ± 9.7 and 115 ± 22.2 μM, respectively (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The IC50 value for di-alanine binding to PepTSh is 72.2 ± 9.7 μM.
source: The IC50 value for tri-alanine, di-alanine and Cys-Gly were 23.7 ± 3.4, 72.2 ± 9.7 and 115 ± 22.2 μM, respectively (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The IC50 value for Cys-Gly binding to PepTSh is 115 ± 22.2 μM.
source: The IC50 value for tri-alanine, di-alanine and Cys-Gly were 23.7 ± 3.4, 72.2 ± 9.7 and 115 ± 22.2 μM, respectively (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The IC50 value for S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH binding to PepTSh is 362 ± 21.8 μM.
source: However, for S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH the IC50 value was 362 ± 21.8 μM, three-fold higher than the Cys-Gly peptide.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: The addition of the thioalcohol group on the cysteine side chain has substantially impaired the recognition and transport of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH versus natural peptides.
source: Our data therefore show that while PepTSh can transport the modified peptide, the addition of the thioalcohol group on the cysteine side chain has substantially impaired the recognition and transport versus natural peptides.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the IC50 data.

claim: A high-resolution co-crystal structure of PepTSh bound to S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH was obtained at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: To gain further insight into the mechanism of substrate binding we successfully obtained a high-resolution co-crystal structure of PepTSh at 2.5 Å resolution, bound to S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH using the in meso crystallisation method (Figure 4A, Table 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure and table.

claim: PepTSh adopts the canonical MFS fold with helices H1-H6 forming the N-terminal bundle and H7-H12 the C-terminal bundle.
source: PepTSh adopts the canonical MFS fold with helices H1-H6 forming the N-terminal bundle and H7-H12 the C-terminal bundle.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: PepTSh was crystallised in an inward open state.
source: PepTSh was crystallised in an inward open state, observed previously for other members of the POT family (Newstead, 2015), wherein the extracellular gate, consisting of helices H1-2 and H7-8 from the N- and C-terminal bundles respectively, is closed and the intracellular gate, consisting of helices H4-5 and H10-11 is open.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure with citation support.

claim: PepTSh contains two additional helices inserted between the N- and C-terminal bundles, termed HA and HB.
source: Similar to other bacterial POT family members, PepTSh contains two additional helices inserted between the N- and C-terminal bundles, termed HA and HB (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure with reference to figures.

claim: PepTSh contains a well-structured β-hairpin motif between helices H7 and H8 on the extracellular side of the membrane.
source: Unlike previous POT structures however, PepTSh also contains a well-structured β-hairpin motif between helices H7 and H8 on the extracellular side of the membrane, extending out in line with the lipid head groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: Monoolein lipid molecules cluster around both the β-hairpin and the cavity created between helices HA and HB with the transporter domain.
source: Interestingly we observed a number of monoolein lipid molecules that cluster around both the β- hairpin and the cavity created between helices HA and HB with the transporter domain.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: The terminal carboxyl group of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH makes two hydrogen bond interactions, one with Tyr41 on H1 and a second interaction to a water molecule (W107).
source: The terminal carboxyl group makes two hydrogen bond interactions, one with Tyr41 on H1 and a second interaction to a water molecule (W107), which links the carboxyl group with Asn347 on H8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: The terminal amino group of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH makes two polar interactions, with a water molecule that sits next to Tyr41 and also to the carbonyl group of Gln344.
source: The terminal amino group makes two further polar interactions, with a water molecule that sits next to Tyr41 and also to the carbonyl group of Gln344, which sits further up on H8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: The thioalcohol moiety of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH points towards the extracellular gate, with the sulphur atom sitting close to Gln310 on H7.
source: In contrast, the thioalcohol moiety points towards the extracellular gate, with the sulphur atom sitting close to Gln310 on H7, whereas the alcohol group extends towards helix H8 making interactions with backbone carbonyl and amide groups of Phe343 and Asn347, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure.

claim: The acyl group of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH extends into a large pocket nestled between helices H7 and H10.
source: The acyl group extends into a large pocket nestled between helices H7 and H10 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the crystal structure with reference to figure.

claim: The S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH peptide adopts a more vertical orientation in PepTSh, similar to the tri-alanine position in PepTSt.
source: Here we see that the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH peptide adopts a more vertical orientation, similar to the tri-alanine position in PepTSt.
evidence: This is stated in the results section comparing structures.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH sits much further up in the binding site compared to the natural peptides captured in PepTSt.
source: A structural overlay of the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH peptide shows that it sits much further up in the binding site compared to the natural peptides captured in PepTSt (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A & B), most likely as a result of the requirement to accommodate the thioalcohol group in the extended pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the results section comparing structures with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Water mediates interactions between peptides and their binding sites in PepTSh.
source: The role of water in mediating interactions between peptides and their binding sites has been previously observed in the ABC transporter binding domains (Tame et al., 1995), albeit for side chain independent binding. A similar mechanism may be employed by PepTSh to facilitate transport of modified peptides by replacing direct interactions between the peptide and the transporter when these are sterically restricted, as we observe with S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation support.

claim: Mutating Tyr41 to phenylalanine or alanine severely reduced transport of di-alanine compared to WT protein.
source: Mutating Tyr41 to phenylalanine or alanine severely reduced transport of di-alanine compared to WT protein (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: Both Tyr41Phe and Tyr41Ala variants had reduced activity for S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH, at about 50% of the wild-type protein.
source: Interestingly, while both Tyr41Phe and Tyr41Ala variants had reduced activity, at about 50% of the wild-type protein (Figure 5B), the phenotype was not as severe as that observed in the liposome based assay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: Recognition of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is less dependent on Tyr41 than di-Ala.
source: We interpret this result to indicate that recognition of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is less dependent on this residue than di-Ala.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mutagenesis data.

claim: The Asn347Ala variant showed reduced uptake of di-Ala.
source: we observed reduced uptake of di-Ala in the Asn347Ala variant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The reduction in activity for Asn347Ala was far more severe in the in vivo assay for S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
source: Interestingly, this reduction was far more severe in the in vivo assay (Figure 5B), indicating that this interaction is more important for transport of the S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH peptide than di-Ala.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: A Tyr411Trp variant showed reduced uptake at ~19% compared to WT.
source: To test the importance of this pocket on S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH transport, we made a Tyr411Trp variant, which would block the cavity. Uptake was noticeably reduced, but still measurable at ~19% compared to WT (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The Tyr411Trp mutation resulted in a large decrease in the biotransformation of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
source: The same mutation resulted in a similar large decrease in the biotransformation of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH, while a Tyr411Ala mutation had wild-type biotransformation rates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to figure showing experimental data.

claim: The hydrophobic pocket in PepTSh plays an important role in facilitating the recognition of the thioalcohol group in the binding pocket.
source: It is clear that the hydrophobic pocket in PepTSh plays an important role in facilitating the recognition of the thioalcohol group in the binding pocket and, as discussed below, is a potential site for inhibitor design.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The production of malodour by humans is an evolutionary ancient olfactory process that likely was involved in mate selection.
source: The production of malodour by humans is an evolutionary ancient olfactory process that likely was involved in mate selection and evolutionary processes that relied on chemical signalling (Stoddart, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Evidence for the microbial origins of chemical signalling molecules is seen in other animals such as foxes, deer, cats and beetles.
source: Evidence for the microbial origins of chemical signalling molecules is also seen in other animals such as foxes, deer, cats and beetles (Wyatt, 2003)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Each of the malodour producing staphylococcal strains have a POT family transporter that is closely related to PepTSh.
source: Each of these strains have a POT family transporter that is closely related to PepTSh (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and we would predict they will also be able to uptake S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to supporting figure.

claim: The POT transporter DtpT is essential for growth on dipeptides and some tripeptides in S. aureus.
source: First, this staphylococci has a similar repertoire of peptide transporters in S. aureus, in that it has a single POT transporter and one Opp ABC transporter, and previous work in S. aureus has demonstrated that the POT transporter, DtpT, is essential for growth on dipeptides and some tripeptides, while the ABC transporter (Opp3) has a function in transporting longer oligopeptides (Hiron et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The ABC transporter Opp3 has a function in transporting longer oligopeptides in S. aureus.
source: First, this staphylococci has a similar repertoire of peptide transporters in S. aureus, in that it has a single POT transporter and one Opp ABC transporter, and previous work in S. aureus has demonstrated that the POT transporter, DtpT, is essential for growth on dipeptides and some tripeptides, while the ABC transporter (Opp3) has a function in transporting longer oligopeptides (Hiron et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is effectively a dipeptide with a highly extended R-group on the first amino acid.
source: Given that S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is effectively a dipeptide with a highly extended R-group on the first amino acid, it is noteworthy that only the promiscuous nature of the POT binding site is able to recognise this ligand.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a characterization of the substrate.

claim: The unusually large structure of the thioalcohol attachment would likely be sterically incompatible with recognition by either OppA or DppA.
source: However, the pocket has evolved to accommodate regular amino acid side chains and the unusually large structure of the thioalcohol attachment would likely be sterically incompatible with recognition by either OppA or DppA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation.

claim: POT transporters have an unusually promiscuous binding site that may play an evolutionary advantageous role in accepting modified peptides as substrates.
source: The data presented here further support the idea that POT transporters have an unusually promiscuous binding site that may play an evolutionary advantageous role in accepting modified peptides as substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The human POT family transporters PepT1 and PepT2 play a role in the absorption and retention of several important classes of drug molecule.
source: Recently, the human POT family transporters, PepT1 and PepT2, have gained additional attention due to their role in the absorption and retention of several important classes of drug molecule (Smith et al., 2013), including peptide modified pro-drugs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Pro-drugs are able to compete with natural peptides for transport via PepT1 and PepT2.
source: Pro-drugs are able to compete with natural peptides for transport via PepT1 and PepT2, and are therefore actively transported into the body (Ganapathy et al., 1998; Gupta et al., 2013; Terada and Inui, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The promiscuous nature of the POT family binding site derives from their ability to recognise peptides in different conformations and through the availability of different specificity pockets.
source: The promiscuous nature of the POT family binding site has been shown to derive, in part, from their ability to recognise peptides in different conformations and through the availability of different specificity pockets, which are able to accommodate chemically different classes of peptides (Newstead, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that specificity pockets can accommodate exotic chemical extensions.
source: Our results here provide the first evidence that specificity pockets can also accommodate exotic chemical extensions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a novel finding.

claim: Water may bridge interactions between the binding site and either the amino or carboxy group of the ligand, increasing the number of conformations a peptide could adopt.
source: In particular, the observation that water may bridge interactions between the binding site and either the amino or carboxy group of the ligand would greatly increase the number of conformations a peptide could adopt in the transporter and still trigger proton coupled transport.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The bacterium will gain a nutritional benefit from the catabolism of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH via the release of both nitrogen and carbon as glycine, pyruvate and ammonia.
source: The bacterium will gain a nutritional benefit from the catabolism of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH via the release of both nitrogen and carbon as glycine, pyruvate and ammonia (Figure 6), which may have been the evolutionary trigger for the adaptation to catabolise this chemical.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to figure.

claim: Asian individuals with single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in ABCC11 have been studied.
source: Asian individuals with single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in ABCC11, the transporters involved in the secretion of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH (Figure 1) have been studied (Nakano et al., 2009; Baumann et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The proportion of Staphylococcus sp. is higher in the underarms of humans that produce the precursor.
source: Recently, a microbiological investigation of individuals with wild-type alleles of ABCC11 compared to heterozygous and double mutant genotypes revealed that the proportion of Staphylococcus sp. is higher in the underarms of humans that produce the precursor (Harker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: The discovery of the transporter and molecular understanding of the mode of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH binding suggests a specific route to develop inhibitors of malodour production.
source: The discovery of the transporter and molecular understanding of the mode of S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH binding now suggests a specific route to develop inhibitors of malodour production by directly inhibiting the transporter SH1446 (Grice, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: Such intervention would not impact on the overall axillar microbiome, but instead specifically target the reduction in body odour production.
source: Importantly, such intervention would not impact on the overall axillar microbiome, but instead specifically target the reduction in body odour production.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a potential application.

claim: The apocrine gland secretes directly into the hair follicle.
source: Thioalcohols are known to be released as a peptide-conjugated precursor from the apocrine gland, which secretes directly into the hair follicle (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to figure.

claim: SG-3M3SH is actively transported by the ATP-binding cassette transporter sub-family C member 11 (ABCC11) into apocrine secretory vesicles.
source: SG-3M3SH is actively transported by the ATP-binding cassette transporter sub-family C member 11 (ABCC11) into apocrine secretory vesicles (Baumann et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption with citation support.

claim: In the secretory vesicle, S-Gly-3M3SH is bio-transformed by γ-glutamyl transferase 1 (GGT1), which cleaves the terminal glutamyl residue generating S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
source: In the secretory vesicle, S-Gly-3M3SH is bio-transformed by γ-glutamyl transferase 1 (GGT1), which cleaves the terminal glutamyl residue generating S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption.

claim: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is secreted to the surface of the skin by apocrine secretion, which characteristically involves pinching off the apical cytoplasm and partial shedding releasing intracellular components into the luminal region of the apocrine gland.
source: S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH is secreted to the surface of the skin by apocrine secretion, which characteristically involves pinching off the apical cytoplasm and partial shedding releasing intracellular components into the luminal region of the apocrine gland. Upon release the cytoplasm may be recovered and repaired and a new cycle of secretion can occur (Farkaš, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1C caption with citation support.

claim: Staphylococcus hominis transport and metabolise cysteinylglycine-3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH) to liberate the odorous volatile 3M3SH.
source: Staphylococcus hominis transport and metabolise cysteinylglycine- 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH) to liberate the odorous volatile 3M3SH, which is one of the major components of axillary malodour.

claim: 3M3SH is one of the major components of axillary malodour.
source: Staphylococcus hominis transport and metabolise cysteinylglycine- 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol (S-Cys-Gly-3M3SH) to liberate the odorous volatile 3M3SH, which is one of the major components of axillary malodour.
